The stereotype of Black women being “loud” comes from a long history of racism and sexism — what scholars sometimes call misogynoir (a specific kind of prejudice against Black women). This stereotype is rooted in several historical forces: • Slavery and Racism: During slavery in the U.S., Black women were dehumanized to justify their mistreatment. They were often portrayed as aggressive or overly emotional to make their resistance to oppression seem unreasonable. • Post-slavery Media and Culture: After emancipation, minstrel shows and early films (like the “mammy” or “sapphire” caricatures) exaggerated Black women as sassy, angry, or loud for entertainment. These depictions stuck in popular culture. • Controlling Narratives: Labeling Black women as “loud” has historically been a way to discredit their anger or assertiveness, especially when they stood up against injustice. Instead of being seen as strong or passionate, they were often ridiculed or dismissed. • Cultural Misunderstandings: Different communication styles also play a role. In many Black communities, expressive speech — animated tone, big gestures — is normal and valued. However, dominant (white) cultural norms have often labeled that expressiveness as “too much” or “loud.” Ultimately, this stereotype is harmful because it tries to silence Black women’s voices or shame them for expressing themselves authentically.

Michael Faraday (1791–1867) was an English scientist whose groundbreaking work in electromagnetism and electrochemistry laid the foundation for modern physics and electrical engineering. Born into a humble family in Newington Butts, England, Faraday had little formal education and began his career as an apprentice bookbinder. His curiosity and self-driven study of science led him to attend lectures by the renowned chemist Humphry Davy, who later offered him a position as his assistant at the Royal Institution. Faraday's experiments led to major discoveries, including electromagnetic induction, the principle behind electric transformers and generators. He also introduced key concepts like the electromagnetic field and electrolysis laws. His discovery of benzene and his work on dielectric materials contributed significantly to chemistry and physics. Despite lacking mathematical training, his intuitive approach to science revolutionized how electricity and magnetism were understood. Faraday was deeply committed to education and public science communication, delivering popular lectures, including the famous Christmas Lectures at the Royal Institution. Though he declined a knighthood and other formal honors, his impact on science was immense, and his work directly influenced later scientists like James Clerk Maxwell.
